name: Amazon
summary: Amazon is a US technology and retail company based in Seattle. Its AI products include the [Amazon Nova](https://aws.amazon.com/ai/generative-ai/nova/) models, the Alexa voice assistant, and AI coding tools.

incidents.title: FTC and DOJ Charge Amazon Over Keeping Children's Alexa Recordings to Train Algorithms
incidents.summary: The FTC and the US Department of Justice charged that Amazon kept children's Alexa voice recordings for years and used them to improve its Alexa algorithm, in violation of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). Amazon agreed to pay a $25 million civil penalty and to delete the data.
incidents.description: In May 2023, the FTC and the US Department of Justice [alleged](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2023/05/ftc-doj-charge-amazon-violating-childrens-privacy-law-keeping-kids-alexa-voice-recordings-forever) that Amazon kept children's Alexa voice recordings and location data for years and used them to improve its Alexa algorithm. They said that this violated the US children's privacy law (COPPA). Under a [court order](https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/cases-proceedings/192-3128-amazoncom-alexa-us-v), Amazon must pay a $25 million civil penalty and delete some of this data.

incidents.title: FTC Charges Amazon's Ring Over Staff Access to Customer Videos and Training Without Consent
incidents.summary: The FTC charged that Amazon's Ring let employees and contractors access customers' private videos, used the videos to train algorithms without consent, and did not stop hackers from taking control of accounts. Ring agreed to pay $5.8 million and to delete data products made from the videos.
incidents.description: [The FTC said](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2023/05/ftc-says-ring-employees-illegally-surveilled-customers-failed-stop-hackers-taking-control-users) that Ring let employees and contractors see customers' private videos and used the videos to train algorithms without consent. It also said that hackers got access to about 55,000 US customer accounts. Under a [court order](https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/cases-proceedings/2023113-ring-llc), Ring paid $5.8 million and must delete data and algorithms made from the videos.

incidents.title: Amazon's Alexa Reportedly Said the 2020 US Election Was Stolen
incidents.summary: The Washington Post reported that Alexa said the 2020 US presidential election was stolen and cited sources such as Rumble and Substack. Amazon said the responses were errors and that it fixed them. Two members of Congress asked Amazon for answers.
incidents.description: [The Washington Post reported](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2023/10/07/amazon-alexa-news-2020-election-misinformation/) that Alexa told users who asked about fraud in the 2020 US presidential election that the election was stolen. The answers reportedly cited sources such as Substack and Rumble. [Amazon said](https://www.seattletimes.com/nation-world/nation/amazons-alexa-has-been-claiming-the-2020-election-was-stolen/) that the answers were errors and that it fixed them. Two members of Congress asked Amazon how Alexa chooses its sources.

incidents.title: Internal Documents Reportedly Say Amazon Q Had Severe Hallucinations and Leaked Confidential Data
incidents.summary: Platformer reported that, days after Amazon announced its Q business chatbot, employees warned that it had "severe hallucinations" and leaked confidential data. Amazon said Q did not leak confidential information.
incidents.description: According to [Platformer](https://www.platformer.news/amazons-q-has-severe-hallucinations/), leaked internal documents said that Amazon Q, a business chatbot in preview, gave false answers and exposed confidential data, such as the locations of AWS data centers. An employee reportedly gave the issue a high severity level. Amazon said that Q did not leak confidential information.

incidents.title: Amazon's Alexa Gave Reasons to Vote for Kamala Harris but Not Donald Trump
incidents.summary: A video showed that Alexa gave reasons to vote for Kamala Harris but refused to give reasons to vote for Donald Trump. Amazon said it was an error that it fixed quickly. Members of Congress asked Amazon for a briefing.
incidents.description: In September 2024, a video showed that Amazon's Alexa listed reasons to vote for Kamala Harris but refused to do the same for Donald Trump. [Amazon said](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/trump-harris-alexa/) that this was an error and that it fixed the error quickly. Members of Congress asked Amazon for an explanation, and [Amazon reportedly added](https://www.foxbusiness.com/politics/amazon-alexas-pro-harris-responses-werent-pre-programmed-source) manual overrides for all candidates.

incidents.title: Attacker Put a Data-Wiping Prompt Into Amazon's Q Developer Extension for VS Code
incidents.summary: An attacker got write access to the open-source repository of the Amazon Q Developer extension and added a prompt that told the AI agent to delete local files and cloud resources. AWS released the change in version 1.84.0. AWS said the code did not run because of a syntax error, and it removed the version (CVE-2025-8217).
incidents.description: [According to AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-015/), an attacker used a GitHub token to add a prompt to the Amazon Q Developer extension for VS Code. The prompt told the AI agent to delete local files and cloud resources, and AWS released it to users in version 1.84.0. AWS said a syntax error stopped the code, and it released version 1.85.0.

timeline.description: A GitHub user committed the prompt to the extension's repository ([BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/amazon-ai-coding-agent-hacked-to-inject-data-wiping-commands/)).

incidents.title: Reports Link AWS and Amazon Retail Outages to Amazon's AI Coding Tools
incidents.summary: The Financial Times reported that at least two AWS outages in late 2025 involved Amazon's own AI coding tools, including the Kiro agent. In March 2026 Amazon held an internal meeting about retail site outages. Amazon said the cause was user error, not AI, and that only one incident involved AI tools.
incidents.description: [The Financial Times reported](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/feb/20/amazon-cloud-outages-ai-tools-amazon-web-services-aws) that Amazon's Kiro coding agent caused a 13-hour interruption to an AWS cost tool in China after it decided to delete and recreate the environment. [Amazon said](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/aws/aws-service-outage-ai-bot-kiro) the cause was user error, not AI, and added required peer review for production access. Amazon also said only one of its later retail site outages involved AI tools.

timeline.description: The Financial Times later reported that the interruption followed changes made by the Kiro agent ([The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/feb/20/amazon-cloud-outages-ai-tools-amazon-web-services-aws)).

incidents.title: AWS Confirmed Prompt Injection Could Make Amazon Q Developer and Kiro Run Commands Without Approval
incidents.summary: In [security bulletin AWS-2025-019](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-019/), AWS confirmed that instructions hidden in files could make Amazon Q Developer run some commands, and make Kiro run code, without human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmation. AWS fixed the issues in July and August 2025. The bulletin does not report use by attackers.
incidents.description: [AWS confirmed](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-019/) that instructions hidden in files could make Amazon Q Developer IDE plugins run commands and the Kiro IDE run code without user approval. AWS released updates that require approval for these actions, with the Kiro fix applying to Supervised mode.

incidents.title: AWS Disclosed Kiro Flaws That Let the Agent Run Code or Send Data Out Without User Approval
incidents.summary: From May to September 2026, AWS published security bulletins for at least four Kiro flaws that went around the user-approval step: crafted content could make the agent write files that ran code or sent workspace data out, or approve tool runs for the user. AWS fixed each flaw. The bulletins do not report use by attackers.
incidents.description: From May to September 2026, AWS disclosed at least four flaws in the Kiro IDE and Kiro CLI that went around the user-approval step. According to AWS, crafted content could make the agent run code or [send workspace data to an external endpoint](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/2026-111-aws/). AWS fixed each flaw, and the bulletins do not report use by attackers.

incidents.title: Researchers Say One Prompt Could Let Attackers Take Over AWS Bedrock AgentCore Agents
incidents.summary: Zenity Labs [said](https://labs.zenity.io/post/agentcorruption-how-a-single-prompt-collapsed-the-entire-cloud-security-model) that one prompt could make an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent fetch its cloud credentials, and that the broad default role then let it run other agents, read their conversations, plant memories and read stored secrets. AWS [told Dark Reading](https://www.darkreading.com/cloud-security/agentcorruption-aws-environments-at-risk-single-prompt) that the research describes documented and expected behavior.
incidents.description: [Zenity Labs said](https://labs.zenity.io/post/agentcorruption-how-a-single-prompt-collapsed-the-entire-cloud-security-model) that a prompt injection could make an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent give its cloud credentials to an attacker. With the broad default role, the attacker could then run other agents in the account and region, read their conversations and read secrets. [AWS said](https://www.darkreading.com/cloud-security/agentcorruption-aws-environments-at-risk-single-prompt) that this is expected behavior, but according to Zenity, AWS later removed these permissions.

timeline.title: Researchers report the broad default role
timeline.description: Zenity Labs sends AWS a second report on the permissions of AgentCore's default role ([Zenity Labs](https://labs.zenity.io/post/agentcorruption-how-a-single-prompt-collapsed-the-entire-cloud-security-model)).
